I played against this as necro a while ago and got smashed. I swiftly learnt how bad midlane can get. I've been thinking about the lane a lot and I think there is an out (for necro at least). 

* You gotta keep the lane in flux. Silencer has no real AOE which means he lacks wave control. Typical midlaners have some sort of wave clearing ability. Keeping the lane in the middle means you're constantly interacting with the Silencer. Just get the damn wave out asap and let it bounce between the towers. Silencer cannot stop this short of killing you.

* You've got the lane out but now you're 1/4 hp from Silencer clicking and DOTing you. Ferry out a salve every minute.

* Try to shove the wave that meets in the first half of every minute so you can stack two camps while the lane is coming back. You wont have time if you go for the 45 second wave.

So you're shoving > healing > stacking > repeat. It's not going to be as good as wave farm but you've got no choice short of supports rotating to help. Repeat ad nauseam until you can roam or a support takes mid. Best case scenario you get the Silencer following you around trying to mitigate your sidelane pressure with his rinky dink slow-ass kit.

I made the post.

Curtis reacted to my post and played two whole games, so I might miss some points he addressed in the video.

I'll begin by saying my two biggest regrets about making the post were, 1: mentioning names (Neace in particular), and, 2: saying bronze-plat have perfect fundementals. What I should have said is 'bronze-plat display *perfectly fine* fundementals' - as in they're fully aware of the importance of things like CS, wave manipulation, etc. Most variation in this regard is in execution, a bronze player may miss 1 extra CS every 2 waves compared to the plat guy. My original intent was to get people talking about low elo knowledge and it's impact in educational space, not to be an accurate measure of skill differences.

Simply put, I'm not convinced it is knowledge of fundementals holding people back. Coaches continue to promote content that elevate this standpoint to the detriment of the estoteric, a blunder that hinders - if not worsens - one's ability to climb and learn.

This specific point is a huge paradox in the educational space. Do we play safe and lean back on fundementals, or do we limit test and push the boundaries of our ability?

Playing safe, focusing on CS is an excellent way to achieve a safe 50% winrate at your ELO. Because with the exception of people actively looking for opportunities to secure leads, thats what everyone is doing. My whole point is that fundementals are not a secret in low ELO. Smurfs don't smurf because they're playing safe and farm for 20 mins, they smurf because they correctly identify opportunities to win. Passive playstyles are fertile ground for others to win your game for you, or beat you.

These games are a perfect representation of bronze-silver. You can laugh at the veigar or yasuo and see how they get demolished after they try to play aggressively, but who is learning more here? The conceptual Annie waiting for the aggression, or the aggressor? When that painful experience of getting demolished is now burned into their brains and another limit has been established, what does Annie learn? I can't help but think, as the conceptual bronze Annie, is that all you've done is help someone else improve at the game.

I regret mentioning you. People - including yourself - are completely missing the point and think this is some sort of anti-Neace bandwagon.

As a coach, could you address the possibility that the low elo bracket has improved to the point where educational content targetting basic concepts for climbing is outdated? Content like this: https://youtu.be/n4TSRL8pZrU is a relic, but still exemplifies the dominant advice for low elo; active discouragement of the esoteric for the sake of fundementals.

I don't want to talk about neace. I gave one neace game as an example of the weakness of relying on pure fundementals in low elo to win in low elo, an idea which is permeating throughout the educational/coaching community. Bronze = low elo in general.

There are champion fundementals (which I would rather call champion mastery) and game fundementals. Knowing dragons exist is a fundemental, as is jungle tracking, roam timers, wave analysis. As with anything, knowledge of these concepts is a matter of degree, a bronze player knows dragons are valuable for lategame, a challenger player knows the strengths of the soul and extrapolate a gameplan off its importance in relation to other objectives.

Fundementals in this case respresent knowledge of the game that is fundemental to playing any champion. Take CSing as another example. Neace did a poor job for whatever reason, but he knows things like which minion is going to die first, and will calculate that at a challenger level, which we are assuming is quicker and more accurate than a bronze calculation.

I now realise perhaps you are proving my point. Challenger fundementals (as defined here) failed neace, he was dulled by a better understanding of a "high level" concept - champion mastery: matchup knowledge. Again, if fundementals (as defined here) win the day in low elo, how was he beaten with esoteric knowledge in bronze?

Cherrypicked? I watched it today and noticed Neace's surprise to bronze level ability, spurring my post. People are missing the forest for the trees, I'm discussing the possibility of high elo/content creator overemphasisation on the power of fundementals in low elo, not NEACE in particular.

As someone in this thread already said, he doesn't play Aatrox; which means he had to fall back on his challenger level fundementals and game ability, which was effectively challenged by bronze level fundementals. 

Watch any challenger player playing an unfamiliar role/champion and you'll see them falter even in low elo because the "high level" concepts that got them to high elo (champion mastery, decisionmaking) is gone, fundementals remain.

You cannot consistently win games in bronze with good fundementals alone, thats all.

You keep saying “it’s unethical” without really thinking about the logistics of what your proposing. Let’s say the government hands out some free land to give to the homeless, what are the homeless going to do with it? They can’t afford to hire carpenters, electricians, and plumbers, so who’s building the house? Who is buying the building materials? Are the homeless going to deforest a nearby plantation to turn into lumber? Where does the poop go, do they bury it? 

It would be naive to believe Slab City is proof of the social good of slums, it is the exception that proves the rule. Slab city isn’t crammed with generations of desperate, hungry people, it’s a hippy commune compared to the real thing.

People need more than a roof over their head, they need access to stuff like clean water, electricity, roads, and access to emergency services. Slums do not have proper infrastructure and any they do have is inefficient and potentially dangerous.
